claim: Deletion of the prolactin receptor (Prlr) from forebrain neurons resulted in failure to maintain normal lactation-induced suppression of estrous cycles.
source: Here, deletion of the prolactin receptor (Prlr) from forebrain neurons or arcuate kisspeptin neurons resulted in failure to maintain normal lactation-induced suppression of estrous cycles.
evidence: The abstract directly states this finding, which is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Deletion of the prolactin receptor (Prlr) from arcuate kisspeptin neurons resulted in failure to maintain normal lactation-induced suppression of estrous cycles.
source: Here, deletion of the prolactin receptor (Prlr) from forebrain neurons or arcuate kisspeptin neurons resulted in failure to maintain normal lactation-induced suppression of estrous cycles.
evidence: The abstract directly states this finding, which is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Kisspeptin immunoreactivity was increased in Prlr knockout mice even in the presence of ongoing suckling stimulation and lactation.
source: Kisspeptin immunoreactivity and pulsatile LH secretion were increased in these mice, even in the presence of ongoing suckling stimulation and lactation.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by immunohistochemistry data in the manuscript.

claim: Pulsatile LH secretion was increased in Prlr knockout mice even in the presence of ongoing suckling stimulation and lactation.
source: Kisspeptin immunoreactivity and pulsatile LH secretion were increased in these mice, even in the presence of ongoing suckling stimulation and lactation.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by LH measurement data in the manuscript.

claim: The normal episodic activity of arcuate kisspeptin neurons is rapidly suppressed in pregnancy.
source: GCaMP fibre photometry of arcuate kisspeptin neurons revealed that the normal episodic activity of these neurons is rapidly suppressed in pregnancy and this was maintained throughout early lactation.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by GCaMP photometry data in the manuscript.

claim: The suppression of episodic activity of arcuate kisspeptin neurons was maintained throughout early lactation.
source: GCaMP fibre photometry of arcuate kisspeptin neurons revealed that the normal episodic activity of these neurons is rapidly suppressed in pregnancy and this was maintained throughout early lactation.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by GCaMP photometry data in the manuscript.

claim: Deletion of Prlr from arcuate kisspeptin neurons resulted in early reactivation of episodic activity of kisspeptin neurons prior to a premature return of reproductive cycles in early lactation.
source: Deletion of Prlr from arcuate kisspeptin neurons resulted in early reactivation of episodic activity of kisspeptin neurons prior to a premature return of reproductive cycles in early lactation.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by GCaMP photometry and estrous cycle monitoring data in the manuscript.

claim: Prolactin action on arcuate kisspeptin neurons is necessary for suppressing fertility during lactation in mice.
source: These observations show dynamic variation in arcuate kisspeptin neuronal activity associated with the hormonal changes of pregnancy and lactation, and provide direct evidence that prolactin action on arcuate kisspeptin neurons is necessary for suppressing fertility during lactation in mice.
evidence: The abstract concludes with this claim, which is supported by the combined experimental data from Prlr deletion studies and photometry recordings.

claim: Lactation is accompanied by a period of infertility in mammals.
source: In mammals, lactation is accompanied by a period of infertility.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in reproductive biology, representing general scientific knowledge.

claim: Lactational infertility establishes appropriate birth spacing to enable maternal metabolic resources to be directed towards caring for the newborn offspring.
source: This adaptive change establishes appropriate birth spacing to enable maternal metabolic resources to be directed towards caring for the newborn offspring, rather than supporting another pregnancy (Short, 1976).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Short, 1976.

claim: Lactational infertility is characterised by a lactation-induced suppression of pulsatile luteinizing hormone (LH) secretion.
source: Lactational infertility is characterised by a lactation-induced suppression of pulsatile luteinizing hormone (LH) secretion, and the temporary loss of the reproductive cycle (in rodents this is exhibited as an extended period of diestrus or anestrus) (McNeilly et al., 1983; Fox and Smith, 1984; McNeilly, 2001; Tsukamura and Maeda, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations (McNeilly et al., 1983; Fox and Smith, 1984; McNeilly, 2001; Tsukamura and Maeda, 2001).

claim: In rodents, lactational infertility is exhibited as an extended period of diestrus or anestrus.
source: Lactational infertility is characterised by a lactation-induced suppression of pulsatile luteinizing hormone (LH) secretion, and the temporary loss of the reproductive cycle (in rodents this is exhibited as an extended period of diestrus or anestrus) (McNeilly et al., 1983; Fox and Smith, 1984; McNeilly, 2001; Tsukamura and Maeda, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations (McNeilly et al., 1983; Fox and Smith, 1984; McNeilly, 2001; Tsukamura and Maeda, 2001).

claim: Lactation is characterised by chronically elevated levels of the anterior pituitary hormone prolactin.
source: Lactation is also characterised by chronically elevated levels of the anterior pituitary hormone prolactin, which is essential for milk production and promotes adaptive changes in maternal physiology and behaviour (Short, 1976; McNeilly et al., 1983; McNeilly, 2001; Tsukamura and Maeda, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations (Short, 1976; McNeilly et al., 1983; McNeilly, 2001; Tsukamura and Maeda, 2001).

claim: Prolactin is essential for milk production.
source: Lactation is also characterised by chronically elevated levels of the anterior pituitary hormone prolactin, which is essential for milk production and promotes adaptive changes in maternal physiology and behaviour (Short, 1976; McNeilly et al., 1983; McNeilly, 2001; Tsukamura and Maeda, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations (Short, 1976; McNeilly et al., 1983; McNeilly, 2001; Tsukamura and Maeda, 2001).

claim: Prolactin promotes adaptive changes in maternal physiology and behaviour.
source: Lactation is also characterised by chronically elevated levels of the anterior pituitary hormone prolactin, which is essential for milk production and promotes adaptive changes in maternal physiology and behaviour (Short, 1976; McNeilly et al., 1983; McNeilly, 2001; Tsukamura and Maeda, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations (Short, 1976; McNeilly et al., 1983; McNeilly, 2001; Tsukamura and Maeda, 2001).

claim: Hyperprolactinaemia is a well-recognised cause of infertility.
source: Despite hyperprolactinaemia being a well-recognised cause of infertility, the specific role that prolactin plays in lactational infertility, as distinct from other suckling- or metabolic-related cues, is currently unclear (McNeilly, 2001; McNeilly, 1997).
evidence: This is stated as a well-recognized fact and supported by citations (McNeilly, 2001; McNeilly, 1997).

claim: The specific role that prolactin plays in lactational infertility, as distinct from other suckling- or metabolic-related cues, is currently unclear.
source: Despite hyperprolactinaemia being a well-recognised cause of infertility, the specific role that prolactin plays in lactational infertility, as distinct from other suckling- or metabolic-related cues, is currently unclear (McNeilly, 2001; McNeilly, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations (McNeilly, 2001; McNeilly, 1997) indicating the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Kisspeptin neurons in the arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus are responsible for the periodic release of gonadotrophin-releasing hormone (GnRH).
source: Recent in vivo studies have confirmed that kisspeptin neurons in the arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus are responsible for the periodic release of gonadotrophin-releasing hormone (GnRH) and subsequent pulsatile LH secretion that drives reproductive function (Clarkson et al., 2017; Han et al., 2019; McQuillan et al., 2019; Moore et al., 2022; Han et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations (Clarkson et al., 2017; Han et al., 2019; McQuillan et al., 2019; Moore et al., 2022; Han et al., 2023).

claim: Kisspeptin neurons in the arcuate nucleus are responsible for subsequent pulsatile LH secretion that drives reproductive function.
source: Recent in vivo studies have confirmed that kisspeptin neurons in the arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus are responsible for the periodic release of gonadotrophin-releasing hormone (GnRH) and subsequent pulsatile LH secretion that drives reproductive function (Clarkson et al., 2017; Han et al., 2019; McQuillan et al., 2019; Moore et al., 2022; Han et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations (Clarkson et al., 2017; Han et al., 2019; McQuillan et al., 2019; Moore et al., 2022; Han et al., 2023).

claim: The arcuate kisspeptin neuronal population exhibits episodes of increased intracellular calcium levels coincident with, and immediately preceding, each pulse of LH secretion in intact and gonadectomised male and female mice.
source: Studies using GCaMP fibre photometry in conscious mice have demonstrated that the arcuate kisspeptin neuronal population exhibits episodes of increased intracellular calcium levels coincident with, and immediately preceding, each pulse of LH secretion in intact and gonadectomised male and female mice (Clarkson et al., 2017; Han et al., 2019; McQuillan et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations (Clarkson et al., 2017; Han et al., 2019; McQuillan et al., 2019).

claim: Individual kisspeptin neurons within the arcuate population act in a coordinated, synchronised, and episodic manner.
source: Miniscope investigations showed that individual kisspeptin neurons within the arcuate population act in a coordinated, synchronised, and episodic manner (Moore et al., 2022; Han et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Moore et al., 2022; Han et al., 2023).

claim: Loss of pulsatile LH secretion during lactation and consequent lactational infertility may be caused by the loss of kisspeptin-mediated stimulation of GnRH secretion.
source: Loss of pulsatile LH secretion during lactation and consequent lactational infertility may be caused by the loss of kisspeptin-mediated stimulation of GnRH secretion (Yamada et al., 2007; Liu et al., 2014; Roa et al., 2006; Ladyman and Woodside, 2014; True et al., 2011; Brown et al., 2014; Xu et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations (Yamada et al., 2007; Liu et al., 2014; Roa et al., 2006; Ladyman and Woodside, 2014; True et al., 2011; Brown et al., 2014; Xu et al., 2009).

claim: Kisspeptin expression is markedly suppressed in lactation.
source: Kisspeptin expression is markedly suppressed in lactation (Yamada et al., 2007; True et al., 2011) and even when exogenously stimulated, kisspeptin neurons are unable to activate GnRH neurons during lactation, likely due to a lack of kisspeptin synthesis (Liu et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Yamada et al., 2007; True et al., 2011).

claim: Even when exogenously stimulated, kisspeptin neurons are unable to activate GnRH neurons during lactation, likely due to a lack of kisspeptin synthesis.
source: Kisspeptin expression is markedly suppressed in lactation (Yamada et al., 2007; True et al., 2011) and even when exogenously stimulated, kisspeptin neurons are unable to activate GnRH neurons during lactation, likely due to a lack of kisspeptin synthesis (Liu et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation (Liu et al., 2014).

claim: Hyperprolactinemia causes infertility.
source: It is well established that hyperprolactinemia causes infertility, and thus, the elevated prolactin present in lactation seems a likely candidate to be involved in suppressing fertility during lactation.
evidence: This is stated as a well-established fact, representing general scientific knowledge.

claim: Prolactin administration acutely suppresses LH secretion.
source: Prolactin administration acutely suppresses LH secretion (Brown et al., 2019), and chronic exposure to elevated prolactin reduces Kiss1 mRNA expression in the arcuate nucleus (Brown et al., 2014; Araujo-Lopes et al., 2014; Sonigo et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation (Brown et al., 2019).

claim: Chronic exposure to elevated prolactin reduces Kiss1 mRNA expression in the arcuate nucleus.
source: Prolactin administration acutely suppresses LH secretion (Brown et al., 2019), and chronic exposure to elevated prolactin reduces Kiss1 mRNA expression in the arcuate nucleus (Brown et al., 2014; Araujo-Lopes et al., 2014; Sonigo et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations (Brown et al., 2014; Araujo-Lopes et al., 2014; Sonigo et al., 2012).

claim: In lactating mice, suppressing endogenous prolactin secretion shortens the period of infertility.
source: In lactating mice, suppressing endogenous prolactin secretion shortens the period of infertility (Hackwell et al., 2023), suggesting that prolactin is important for maintaining the suppression of pulsatile LH secretion during lactation.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation (Hackwell et al., 2023).

claim: Control Prlrlox/lox mice showed a marked reduction in kisspeptin cell body immunoreactivity in the RP3V of lactating compared to intact, diestrous, nulligravid, non-lactating mice (p=0.0100).
source: Control Prlrlox/lox mice showed a marked reduction in kisspeptin cell body immunoreactivity in the RP3V of lactating compared to intact, diestrous, nulligravid, non-lactating (henceforth termed NL) mice (p=0.0100, Post hoc Tukey's multiple comparisons test, Figure 1A and C; source data is available in supplementary file: Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and C with statistical analysis.

claim: In Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre mice the lactation-induced suppression of kisspeptin cell bodies in the RP3V was absent (p=0.6409).
source: In contrast, in Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre mice the lactation-induced suppression of kisspeptin cell bodies in the RP3V was absent (p=0.6409, Post hoc Tukey's multiple comparisons test; interaction between reproductive state and genotype p=0.0034, two-way ANOVA, Figure 1A and C;).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and C with statistical analysis.

claim: Fibre density in the arcuate nucleus was significantly increased in lactating Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre mice compared to lactating Prlrlox/lox controls (p=0.0020).
source: Fibre density in the arcuate nucleus was significantly increased in lactating Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre mice compared to lactating Prlrlox/lox controls (p=0.0020, unpaired two-tailed t-test, measured as percentage voxels within the region of interest, Figure 1B and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and D with statistical analysis.

claim: Lactating Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre mice resume estrous cycles significantly earlier (100% within 6–10 d of lactation) than lactating Prlrlox/lox controls (p≤0.0001).
source: Estrous cycles during lactation were significantly altered by deletion of Prlr in the forebrain, with all Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre mice showing a return to estrus between day 6 and day 10 of lactation (Figure 1E), while, as normal, estrus did not occur until day 20 (after weaning) in control Prlrlox/lox mice (p≤0.0001, log-rank (Mantel-Cox) test, Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E with statistical analysis.

claim: No differences in litter weight gain from day 3 to day 8 of lactation were observed between Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre and control groups (p=0.3282).
source: No differences in litter weight gain from day 3 to day 8 of lactation were observed in either group (p=0.3282, mixed analysis test, Figure 1—figure supplement 2), indicating that the suckling stimulus that mice received and lactation itself was maintained in the absence of Prlr expression in Camk2a expressing neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 with statistical analysis.

claim: The suckling stimulus and lactation itself was maintained in the absence of Prlr expression in Camk2a expressing neurons.
source: No differences in litter weight gain from day 3 to day 8 of lactation were observed in either group (p=0.3282, mixed analysis test, Figure 1—figure supplement 2), indicating that the suckling stimulus that mice received and lactation itself was maintained in the absence of Prlr expression in Camk2a expressing neurons.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the litter weight gain data.

claim: Prolactin action in the brain is absolutely required for the lactation-induced suppression of kisspeptin expression in mice.
source: Collectively, these data show that prolactin action in the brain is absolutely required for the lactation-induced suppression of kisspeptin expression and to maintain lactational infertility in mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined experimental data on kisspeptin expression and estrous cycles.

claim: Prolactin action in the brain is absolutely required to maintain lactational infertility in mice.
source: Collectively, these data show that prolactin action in the brain is absolutely required for the lactation-induced suppression of kisspeptin expression and to maintain lactational infertility in mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined experimental data on kisspeptin expression and estrous cycles.

claim: Vehicle-treated Prlrlox/lox control mice showed the expected near complete absence of pulsatile LH secretion during lactation.
source: Vehicle-treated Prlrlox/lox control mice showed the expected near complete absence of pulsatile LH secretion during lactation (Figure 2A and B; source data is available in supplementary file: Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Nearly all Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre mice showed a lack of the normal lactation-induced suppression of pulsatile LH secretion demonstrated by a significant increase in frequency of LH pulses compared to controls (effect of genotype p=0.0024).
source: In contrast, nearly all Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre mice showed a lack of the normal lactation-induced suppression of pulsatile LH secretion demonstrated by a significant increase in frequency of LH pulses compared to controls (effect of genotype p=0.0024, two-way ANOVA with Tukey's multiple comparisons test, Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and B with statistical analysis.

claim: There was no effect of mifepristone on the pattern of LH secretion.
source: There was no effect of mifepristone on the pattern of LH secretion, suggesting that progesterone action is not required for the suppression of LH secretion (LH pulse frequency (interaction genotype x treatment p=0.2807; treatment p=0.8558; Figure 2B); mean LH levels (interaction genotype x treatment p=0.8572; treatment p=0.8457; Figure 2C); two-way ANOVA with Tukey's multiple comparisons test).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and C with statistical analysis.

claim: Progesterone action is not required for the suppression of LH secretion during lactation.
source: There was no effect of mifepristone on the pattern of LH secretion, suggesting that progesterone action is not required for the suppression of LH secretion (LH pulse frequency (interaction genotype x treatment p=0.2807; treatment p=0.8558; Figure 2B); mean LH levels (interaction genotype x treatment p=0.8572; treatment p=0.8457; Figure 2C); two-way ANOVA with Tukey's multiple comparisons test).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the mifepristone treatment data.

claim: Prolactin is the primary signal responsible for the suppression of pulsatile LH secretion during lactation in mice.
source: These data indicate that prolactin is the primary signal responsible for the suppression of pulsatile LH secretion during lactation in mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined experimental data on LH secretion in Prlr knockout mice.

claim: Arcuate kisspeptin photometry recordings were characterised by discrete synchronised events (SEs) of elevated intracellular calcium.
source: As can be seen in Figure 4—source data 1 is available in supplementary file: Figure 4—source data 1, arcuate kisspeptin photometry recordings were characterised by discrete synchronised events (SEs) of elevated intracellular calcium (indicative of synchronous activity of the kisspeptin population), with each SE consistently correlating to a single pulse of LH secretion in the minutes following (p≤0.0001, chi-squared test).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 with statistical analysis.

claim: Each SE consistently correlates to a single pulse of LH secretion in the minutes following (p≤0.0001).
source: As can be seen in Figure 4—source data 1 is available in supplementary file: Figure 4—source data 1, arcuate kisspeptin photometry recordings were characterised by discrete synchronised events (SEs) of elevated intracellular calcium (indicative of synchronous activity of the kisspeptin population), with each SE consistently correlating to a single pulse of LH secretion in the minutes following (p≤0.0001, chi-squared test).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 with statistical analysis.

claim: Periodic SEs occur about once per hour (1.25±0.25 /hr) in diestrous mice.
source: These were observed to be at a similar rate to that described previously in diestrous mice using GCaMP photometry in a different Kiss1 mouse line (McQuillan et al., 2019), with periodic SEs occurring about once per hour (1.25±0.25 /hr; Figures 3 and 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3 and 4B and comparison to previous work (McQuillan et al., 2019).

claim: The activity of the arcuate kisspeptin population in Kiss1Cre mice dynamically changed depending on the reproductive state of the mouse (p=0.0040).
source: The activity of the arcuate kisspeptin population in Kiss1Cre mice dynamically changed depending on the reproductive state of the mouse (p=0.0040, mixed-effect analysis, Figures 3 and 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3 and 4B with statistical analysis.

claim: On day 4 of pregnancy, SE frequency had markedly decreased (0.29±0.14 /hr).
source: On day 4 of pregnancy, SE frequency had markedly decreased (0.29±0.14 /hr; Figures 3 and 4B), indicating an early reduction in activity of arcuate kisspeptin neurons during pregnancy.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3 and 4B.

claim: By day 14 of pregnancy, no SEs were seen (0±0 /hr).
source: By day 14 of pregnancy, no SEs were seen (0±0 /hr; Figures 3 and 4B) and this was confirmed by a lack of pulsatile LH secretion (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3 and 4B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: In late pregnancy (day 18), low amplitude SEs were observed at similar frequencies to NL levels (2.18±1.20 /hr).
source: In late pregnancy (day 18), neuronal activity was monitored for 14 hr, during which time low amplitude, SEs were unexpectedly observed at similar frequencies to NL levels (2.18±1.20 /hr; Figures 3 and 4B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3 and 4B-C.

claim: In early lactation (day 7), the episodic activity of arcuate kisspeptin neurons was absent (0±0 /hr).
source: Evaluation of activity of arcuate kisspeptin neurons during lactation showed complete suppression of activity on day 7 of lactation with a corresponding absence of pulsatile LH secretion (0±0 /hr; Figures 3 and 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3 and 4B.

claim: On day 7 of lactation there was a corresponding absence of pulsatile LH secretion.
source: Evaluation of activity of arcuate kisspeptin neurons during lactation showed complete suppression of activity on day 7 of lactation with a corresponding absence of pulsatile LH secretion (0±0 /hr; Figures 3 and 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3 and 4B.

claim: This lactation-induced suppression of activity was partially relieved by day 14 of lactation (0.58±0.08 /hr).
source: This lactation-induced suppression of activity was partially relieved by day 14 of lactation (0.58±0.08 /hr; Figures 3 and 4B), with low frequency SEs again corresponding to low frequency pulsatile LH secretion.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3 and 4B.

claim: On day 14 of lactation, low frequency SEs corresponded to low frequency pulsatile LH secretion.
source: This lactation-induced suppression of activity was partially relieved by day 14 of lactation (0.58±0.08 /hr; Figures 3 and 4B), with low frequency SEs again corresponding to low frequency pulsatile LH secretion.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3 and 4B.

claim: Further increases in SE frequency were seen on day 18 of lactation (0.85±0.10 /hr).
source: Further increases in SE frequency were seen on day 18 of lactation (0.85±0.10 /hr; Figures 3 and 4B), including an increase in baseline activity, similar to that seen in late pregnancy, and by 24 hr after weaning (day 22 postpartum) the frequency of SEs had returned to close to non-pregnant levels (1.38±0.11 /hr; Figures 3 and 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3 and 4B.

claim: By 24 hr after weaning (day 22 postpartum) the frequency of SEs had returned to close to non-pregnant levels (1.38±0.11 /hr).
source: Further increases in SE frequency were seen on day 18 of lactation (0.85±0.10 /hr; Figures 3 and 4B), including an increase in baseline activity, similar to that seen in late pregnancy, and by 24 hr after weaning (day 22 postpartum) the frequency of SEs had returned to close to non-pregnant levels (1.38±0.11 /hr; Figures 3 and 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3 and 4B.

claim: SE frequency remained unchanged on the day of the first diestrus following a return to estrous cycles after weaning (1.67±0.24 /hr).
source: SE frequency remained unchanged on the day of the first diestrus following a return to estrous cycles after weaning (1.67±0.24 /hr; Figures 3 and 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3 and 4B.

claim: Ten days post-ovariectomy (OVX), clusters of high amplitude arcuate kisspeptin population activity were observed (4.78±0.22 /hr).
source: Ten days post-ovariectomy (OVX), clusters of high amplitude arcuate kisspeptin population activity were observed (4.78±0.22 /hr; Figures 3 and 4B), consistent with previous reports following OVX in nulliparous mice (McQuillan et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3 and 4B and comparison to previous work (McQuillan et al., 2022).

claim: There was early resumption of estrous cycles in Prlrlox/lox/Kiss1Cre mice during lactation (63% showing estrus by day 10 of lactation and 83% by day 19 lactation) compared to Prlrlox/lox controls (4% by day 19 lactation) (p≤0.0001).
source: Similar to the data from Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre mice, there was early resumption of estrous cycles in Prlrlox/lox/Kiss1Cre mice during lactation (63% showing estrus by day 10 of lactation and 83% by day 19 lactation) compared to Prlrlox/lox controls (4% by day 19 lactation) (p≤0.0001, log-rank (Mantel-Cox) test, Figure 6A; source data is available in supplementary file: Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A with statistical analysis.

claim: No difference in litter weight gain during lactation was observed between Prlrlox/lox/Kiss1Cre and control groups indicating that suckling and/or lactation itself was not impaired (day 3–20 lactation weight gain, p=0.6404).
source: No difference in litter weight gain during lactation was observed in either group indicating that suckling and/or lactation itself was not impaired (day 3–20 lactation weight gain, p=0.6404, two-way ANOVA, Figure 6—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2D with statistical analysis.

claim: In vivo, GCaMP fibre photometry in Prlrlox/lox/Kiss1Cre mice showed early reactivation of the arcuate kisspeptin population by day 5 of lactation.
source: In vivo, GCaMP fibre photometry in Prlrlox/lox/Kiss1Cre mice showed early reactivation of the arcuate kisspeptin population by day 5 of lactation (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Early reactivation of arcuate kisspeptin neurons was accompanied by a clear return to estrus within early lactation in four out of five Prlrlox/lox/Kiss1Cre mice.
source: This was accompanied by a clear return to estrus within this early lactation window in four out of five mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the photometry and estrous cycle monitoring studies.

claim: Prolactin action specifically on arcuate kisspeptin neurons is responsible for maintaining suppression of those neurons during lactation in mice.
source: These data demonstrate, in mice, that prolactin action specifically on arcuate kisspeptin neurons is responsible for maintaining suppression of those neurons, and thereby fertility, during lactation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined experimental data on Prlr deletion in kisspeptin neurons.

claim: Prolactin action on arcuate kisspeptin neurons is necessary for lactation-induced infertility in mice.
source: We demonstrate here that prolactin action in arcuate kisspeptin neurons is necessary for the maintained suppression of fertility during lactation in mice.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by all the experimental data presented.

claim: Neuron-specific Prlr deletion (Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre) resulted in the premature return to estrus in early lactation, even in the presence of the ongoing suckling stimulus and the full metabolic consequences of milk production.
source: Neuron-specific Prlr deletion (Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre) resulted in the premature return to estrus in early lactation, even in the presence of the ongoing suckling stimulus and the full metabolic consequences of milk production.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data on estrous cycles and litter weight gain in Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre mice.

claim: Accompanying the resumption of estrus in Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre mice was an absence of the normal lactation-induced reduction in kisspeptin immunoreactivity.
source: Accompanying the resumption of estrus was an absence of the normal lactation-induced reduction in kisspeptin immunoreactivity (Yamada et al., 2007; True et al., 2011; Araujo-Lopes et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by the immunohistochemistry data and citations to previous work (Yamada et al., 2007; True et al., 2011; Araujo-Lopes et al., 2014).

claim: Pulsatile LH secretion was observed on day 5 of lactation in Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre mice prior to the premature estrus when it would normally have been completely absent.
source: Pulsatile LH secretion was also observed on day 5 of lactation prior to the premature estrus when it would normally have been completely absent (Bohnet and Schneider, 1977; McNeilly, 1979; McNeilly et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by the LH measurement data and citations to previous work (Bohnet and Schneider, 1977; McNeilly, 1979; McNeilly et al., 1994).

claim: The data show an immediate suppression of the activity of arcuate kisspeptin neuronal activity during pregnancy.
source: The data show an immediate suppression of the activity of arcuate kisspeptin neuronal activity during pregnancy, and this is maintained throughout most of the lactation, apart from a brief window of reactivation immediately prior to parturition.
evidence: This claim is supported by the longitudinal GCaMP photometry data across pregnancy and lactation.

claim: The suppression of arcuate kisspeptin neuronal activity is maintained throughout most of the lactation, apart from a brief window of reactivation immediately prior to parturition.
source: The data show an immediate suppression of the activity of arcuate kisspeptin neuronal activity during pregnancy, and this is maintained throughout most of the lactation, apart from a brief window of reactivation immediately prior to parturition.
evidence: This claim is supported by the longitudinal GCaMP photometry data across pregnancy and lactation.

claim: Deleting Prlr specifically from arcuate kisspeptin neurons (Prlrlox/lox/Kiss1Cre) prevented the suppression of activity in early lactation, resulting in premature induction of episodic activation of kisspeptin neurons, and early onset of estrus.
source: Deleting Prlr specifically from arcuate kisspeptin neurons (Prlrlox/lox/Kiss1Cre) prevented the suppression of activity in early lactation, resulting in premature induction of episodic activation of kisspeptin neurons, and early onset of estrus.
evidence: This claim is supported by the GCaMP photometry and estrous cycle data in Prlrlox/lox/Kiss1Cre mice.

claim: Arcuate kisspeptin neurons form the GnRH 'pulse generator,' and hence drive the pulsatile release of GnRH from the hypothalamus and consequent pulsatile secretion of LH from the pituitary that is required for fertility.
source: It is now well established that arcuate kisspeptin neurons form the GnRH 'pulse generator,' and hence drive the pulsatile release of GnRH from the hypothalamus and consequent pulsatile secretion of LH from the pituitary that is required for fertility (Herbison, 2018; de Roux et al., 2003; Seminara et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Herbison, 2018; de Roux et al., 2003; Seminara et al., 2003) and represents established scientific knowledge.

claim: This is the first study to monitor the activity of the arcuate kisspeptin neurons across different reproductive states in the same animal.
source: This is the first study to monitor the activity of the arcuate kisspeptin neurons across different reproductive states in the same animal, and the data largely match previously described patterns of LH secretion (McNeilly, 1979; Morishige et al., 1973).
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the study approach.

claim: The data largely match previously described patterns of LH secretion.
source: This is the first study to monitor the activity of the arcuate kisspeptin neurons across different reproductive states in the same animal, and the data largely match previously described patterns of LH secretion (McNeilly, 1979; Morishige et al., 1973).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison to previous work (McNeilly, 1979; Morishige et al., 1973).

claim: The abrupt decrease in arcuate kisspeptin activity in early pregnancy is likely caused by rising levels of progesterone.
source: The abrupt decrease in arcuate kisspeptin activity in early pregnancy is likely caused by rising levels of progesterone, known to profoundly suppress the activity of arcuate kisspeptin neurons and LH secretion (McQuillan et al., 2019; Goodman and Karsch, 1980; Skinner et al., 1998).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations (McQuillan et al., 2019; Goodman and Karsch, 1980; Skinner et al., 1998).

claim: Progesterone is known to profoundly suppress the activity of arcuate kisspeptin neurons and LH secretion.
source: The abrupt decrease in arcuate kisspeptin activity in early pregnancy is likely caused by rising levels of progesterone, known to profoundly suppress the activity of arcuate kisspeptin neurons and LH secretion (McQuillan et al., 2019; Goodman and Karsch, 1980; Skinner et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations (McQuillan et al., 2019; Goodman and Karsch, 1980; Skinner et al., 1998).

claim: Progesterone is elevated throughout pregnancy, gradually increasing until luteolysis and progesterone withdrawal occur in the lead-up to parturition.
source: Progesterone is elevated throughout pregnancy, gradually increasing until luteolysis and progesterone withdrawal occur in the lead-up to parturition (Virgo and Bellward, 1974; Pointis et al., 1981; Bridges, 1984; Sugimoto et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Virgo and Bellward, 1974; Pointis et al., 1981; Bridges, 1984; Sugimoto et al., 1997).

claim: The transient reactivation of the arcuate kisspeptin neurons in the night between days 18 and 19 of pregnancy is likely associated with progesterone withdrawal in late pregnancy.
source: It seems likely that this pattern of activity is associated with progesterone withdrawal in late pregnancy and may be important in stimulating follicular growth leading up to a postpartum ovulation (Thapa et al., 1988; Zakar and Hertelendy, 2007).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations (Thapa et al., 1988; Zakar and Hertelendy, 2007).

claim: The transient reactivation of arcuate kisspeptin neurons in late pregnancy may be important in stimulating follicular growth leading up to a postpartum ovulation.
source: It seems likely that this pattern of activity is associated with progesterone withdrawal in late pregnancy and may be important in stimulating follicular growth leading up to a postpartum ovulation (Thapa et al., 1988; Zakar and Hertelendy, 2007).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations (Thapa et al., 1988; Zakar and Hertelendy, 2007).

claim: The increase in arcuate kisspeptin population activity during late lactation mirrors the increase in LH levels that has been reported as lactation progresses.
source: This increase in arcuate kisspeptin population activity during late lactation mirrors the increase in LH levels that has been reported as lactation progresses (Rolland et al., 1975).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison to previous work (Rolland et al., 1975).

claim: Overall patterns of SE activity rapidly returned to normal diestrus levels soon after weaning.
source: Overall patterns of SE activity rapidly returned to normal diestrus levels soon after weaning (Rolland et al., 1975).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data and comparison to previous work (Rolland et al., 1975).

claim: Prolactin action in arcuate kisspeptin neurons is necessary to sustain lactational infertility in mice.
source: These data clearly show that prolactin action in arcuate kisspeptin neurons is necessary to sustain lactational infertility in mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined experimental data on Prlr deletion in kisspeptin neurons.

claim: The observed disruption of lactational infertility in Prlrlox/lox/Kiss1Cre mice is particularly remarkable given that Prlr deletion is restricted to arcuate kisspeptin neurons in this model.
source: The observed disruption of lactational infertility in Prlrlox/lox/Kiss1Cre mice is particularly remarkable given that Prlr deletion is restricted to arcuate kisspeptin neurons in this model (Brown et al., 2019), and prolactin action on RP3V kisspeptin neurons (Sonigo et al., 2012; Kokay et al., 2011) and on gonadotrophs in the pituitary gland (Hodson et al., 2010; Tortonese et al., 1998; Henderson et al., 2008) are unaffected.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the significance of the findings, supported by citations (Brown et al., 2019; Sonigo et al., 2012; Kokay et al., 2011; Hodson et al., 2010; Tortonese et al., 1998; Henderson et al., 2008).

claim: The indispensable role of prolactin in mediating lactation-induced infertility in the mouse is surprising, given the consensus of much work in other species concluding that other factors may be more important.
source: The indispensable role of prolactin in mediating lactation-induced infertility in the mouse is surprising, given the consensus of much work in other species concluding that other factors may be more important (see McNeilly, 2001; McNeilly, 1997; Tay et al., 1996; Díaz et al., 1989; Woodside and Jans, 1995).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of previous literature, supported by citations (McNeilly, 2001; McNeilly, 1997; Tay et al., 1996; Díaz et al., 1989; Woodside and Jans, 1995).

claim: There may be a level of redundancy amongst contributing factors across all species, including ovarian hormones, metabolic cues, and neural inputs of suckling.
source: This may reflect a level of redundancy amongst contributing factors across all species, including ovarian hormones, metabolic cues, and neural inputs of suckling.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanisms underlying lactational infertility across species.

claim: The conditional deletion approach distinguishes prolactin action from the neurogenic effects of suckling without altering the process of lactation itself.
source: Notably, the conditional deletion approach described here distinguishes prolactin action from the neurogenic effects of suckling without altering the process of lactation itself.
evidence: This is a statement about the methodological advantage of the approach used in the study.

claim: This approach avoids the potential confounding effects of using dopamine agonists to suppress prolactin, given that dopamine can directly inhibit GnRH neuronal activity.
source: Moreover, this approach avoids the potential confounding effects of using dopamine agonists to suppress prolactin (Maeda et al., 1990; Smith, 1978), given that dopamine can directly inhibit GnRH neuronal activity (Liu and Herbison, 2013).
evidence: This is a statement about the methodological advantage of the approach, supported by citations (Maeda et al., 1990; Smith, 1978; Liu and Herbison, 2013).

claim: The global deletion of Prlr (Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre) was more effective at inducing the return to estrus during lactation (in 100% of mice by day 10) compared to the arcuate kisspeptin-specific model (63% by day 10, and 83% by day 19).
source: While the effects of widespread neuronal deletion (Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre) on fertility were largely recapitulated by the arcuate kisspeptin-specific model (Prlrlox/lox/Kiss1Cre), it was apparent that the global deletion was more effective at inducing the return to estrus during lactation (in 100% of Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre mice by day 10), compared to the arcuate kisspeptin-specific model (63% by day 10, and 83% by day 19).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of the experimental data from the two different knockout models.

claim: The difference in effectiveness between global and kisspeptin-specific Prlr deletion may be due to the absence of lactation-induced suppression of Kiss1 expression in RP3V kisspeptin neurons of Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre mice.
source: This may be due to the absence of lactation-induced suppression of Kiss1 expression in RP3V kisspeptin neurons of Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre mice.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism underlying the difference between the two knockout models.

claim: Other populations of prolactin-sensitive neurons, such as GABA or dopamine neurons, may contribute to suppressing estrous cycles during lactation.
source: Similarly, we cannot rule out the possibility that other populations of prolactin-sensitive neurons, such as GABA or dopamine neurons (Kokay et al., 2011), may contribute to suppressing estrous cycles during lactation.
evidence: This is speculation about other potential mechanisms, supported by a citation (Kokay et al., 2011).

claim: Given that hyperprolactinemia induces infertility in many other mammalian species, including humans, it is possible that a conserved mechanism could be contributing to lactational infertility in these species.
source: Given that hyperprolactinemia induces infertility in many other mammalian species, including humans (Sonigo et al., 2012; Hackwell et al., 2023; Greer et al., 1980; Evans et al., 1982; Koike et al., 1991; Patel and Bamigboye, 2007; Cohen-Becker et al., 1986; Sarkar and Yen, 1985; Fox et al., 1987; Park et al., 1993; Park and Selmanoff, 1991; Grattan et al., 2007), it is possible that a conserved mechanism could be contributing to lactational infertility in these species.
evidence: This is speculation about the broader implications of the findings, supported by multiple citations (Sonigo et al., 2012; Hackwell et al., 2023; Greer et al., 1980; Evans et al., 1982; Koike et al., 1991; Patel and Bamigboye, 2007; Cohen-Becker et al., 1986; Sarkar and Yen, 1985; Fox et al., 1987; Park et al., 1993; Park and Selmanoff, 1991; Grattan et al., 2007).

claim: Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre mice showed a significant decrease in the percentage of Kiss1-expressing cells co-expressing Prlr compared to controls in both the RP3V (p≤0.0001) and arcuate nucleus (p=0.0009).
source: Prlrlox/lox/Camk2aCre mice showed a significant decrease in the percentage of Kiss1-expressing cells co-expressing Prlr compared to controls in both the RP3V (p≤0.0001) and arcuate nucleus (p=0.0009) (unpaired two-tailed t-tests, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAscope data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-D with statistical analysis.

claim: Prlrlox/lox/Kiss1Cre mice showed a significant decrease in the percentage of Kiss1-expressing cells co-expressing Prlr compared to controls in the arcuate nucleus (p ≤ 0.0001).
source: RNAscope in-situ hybridisation (as described above) was done to confirm knockdown in a subgroup of these mice, with Prlrlox/lox/Kiss1Cre mice showing a significant decrease in the percentage of Kiss1-expressing cells co-expressing Prlr compared to controls in the arcuate nucleus (p ≤ 0.0001, unpaired two-tailed t-test, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B; Prlrlox/lox n=6, Prlrlox/lox/Kiss1Cre n=7).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAscope data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-B with statistical analysis.

claim: Each time an SE was seen during a recording with blood sampling, pulsatile secretion of LH was also observed, with 100% correlation (p≤0.0001; 73 out of 73 SEs observed led to an LH pulse).
source: When fibre photometry was paired with serial blood sampling for pulsatile LH secretion, the relationship between SEs and LH pulses was examined. Each time an SE was seen during a recording with blood sampling, pulsatile secretion of LH was also observed, with 100% correlation (p≤0.0001, chi-squared test; 73 out of 73 SEs observed led to an LH pulse).
evidence: This claim is supported by paired photometry and blood sampling data shown in Figure 4A with statistical analysis.

claim: No difference was seen between the frequency of SEs (per 60 min) in the NL versus day 18/19 pregnancy (p=0.4063).
source: (C) No difference was seen between the frequency of SEs (per 60 min) in the NL (diestrus, nulligravid, non-lactating) versus day 18/19 pregnancy (p=0.4063, paired two-tailed t-test), however, a significant decrease in relative SE amplitude is seen (D; p=0.0141, paired two-tailed t test).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C with statistical analysis.

claim: A significant decrease in relative SE amplitude is seen between NL and day 18/19 pregnancy (p=0.0141).
source: (C) No difference was seen between the frequency of SEs (per 60 min) in the NL (diestrus, nulligravid, non-lactating) versus day 18/19 pregnancy (p=0.4063, paired two-tailed t-test), however, a significant decrease in relative SE amplitude is seen (D; p=0.0141, paired two-tailed t test).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D with statistical analysis.
